title: U.S. Military Confirms Complete Troop Withdrawal from Iraq, Ending Long‑Running Deployment
body:
The United States has officially concluded its 12‑year military presence in Iraq, pulling the last of its troops and equipment from the country in a coordinated exit that marks the end of the campaign launched to defeat the Islamic State (IS) group. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed Wednesday that the final convoy of American forces crossed the border, ending a deployment that began in 2014 when U.S. airstrikes and advisors were dispatched to support Iraqi forces battling the extremist organization. The withdrawal, described by officials as “orderly and complete,” signals a new chapter in Iraq’s security landscape and tests the resilience of the Iraqi government and its allies.

The mission that began under the Obama administration evolved dramatically over the years. Initially, a modest contingent of special‑operations personnel and air‑power assets was tasked with halting IS’s rapid advance across Mosul and the surrounding regions. By 2017, the U.S. had expanded its role, deploying thousands of troops to train, advise, and assist Iraqi security forces, while conducting a sustained bombing campaign that crippled IS’s command structure. The effort culminated in the liberation of Mosul in 2017 and the eventual territorial defeat of IS by March 2019. Yet, a residual U.S. presence remained to provide counter‑terrorism support, intelligence sharing, and to protect American diplomatic facilities.

The decision to fully withdraw was shaped by a confluence of strategic and political factors. Domestically, the Biden administration has faced mounting pressure to end “forever wars” and reallocate resources to emerging challenges in the Indo‑Pacific and cyber domains. In Baghdad, Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al‑Sudani’s government has repeatedly called for the removal of foreign troops, asserting that Iraq must assume full responsibility for its own security. At the same time, regional dynamics—particularly Iran’s growing influence in Iraq’s political and militia spheres—have complicated the calculus for Washington, prompting a reassessment of how best to balance counter‑terrorism objectives with the risk of entanglement in proxy conflicts.

Analysts caution that the departure does not guarantee a permanent end to IS‑related violence. Although the group has lost its territorial foothold, its ideology endures, and affiliates continue to conduct insurgent attacks across the Middle East. Iraq’s security forces, bolstered by years of U.S. training, still confront a fragmented landscape of militias, sectarian tensions, and economic distress that could be exploited by extremist elements. Moreover, the vacuum left by American troops may embolden Iran‑backed paramilitary groups, which have historically operated with a degree of autonomy and have been both partners and rivals in the fight against IS.

Regional partners are watching the withdrawal closely. Turkey, which shares a volatile border with Iraq and has its own concerns about Kurdish militias, has expressed readiness to cooperate on border security, while Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have signaled a willingness to increase intelligence and logistical support to Iraqi forces. The United Nations, which has been monitoring the humanitarian fallout from the conflict, urged the international community to sustain aid and development programs to address the underlying grievances that fuel radicalization.

Looking ahead, the United States is likely to maintain a limited footprint in Iraq through diplomatic channels, intelligence cooperation, and occasional counter‑terrorism operations, ensuring that it can respond swiftly to any resurgence of extremist activity. The full withdrawal also places a premium on Iraq’s ability to forge a cohesive national security strategy that integrates its army, police, and civil institutions while navigating the complex web of regional influences. As Baghdad assumes sole responsibility for its security, the coming months will test the durability of the gains achieved against IS and the capacity of Iraq’s leaders to steer the nation toward a more stable and self‑reliant future.
